PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 81 — Lesson 105: Osteoarthritis Management

FNP-level goal: Diagnose osteoarthritis (OA) in clinical context, identify alternative or urgent joint pathology, build an individualized function-centered nonoperative plan, use medication safely, and recognize when orthopedic or other specialty referral is appropriate.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize the typical clinical pattern of hand, knee, and hip OA while maintaining a differential for inflammatory, infectious, crystal, traumatic, referred, and neuropathic causes.
  • Identify an acutely hot swollen joint, systemic illness, fracture concern, or neurovascular compromise as urgent—not routine OA—problems.
  • Assess pain, stiffness, function, gait, falls, work/caregiver demands, mood, sleep, weight, comorbidities, and patient goals.
  • Integrate exercise, self-management, weight support when relevant, assistive devices, bracing, and medication safety into a practical care plan.
  • Explain when imaging, injection planning, rehabilitation, and surgical consultation may be useful.

Part 1 — OA Is a Clinical and Functional Diagnosis

OA is a whole-joint disorder involving cartilage, subchondral bone, synovium, ligaments, muscle, and biomechanics. Typical symptoms include activity-related joint pain, short-lived stiffness after rest, reduced range of motion, crepitus, bony enlargement, and progressive functional limitation. Pain severity does not always match radiographic severity. A high-quality diagnosis combines history, examination, risk factors, function, and selected imaging when it will change management.

Ask the patient what they cannot do: climb stairs, stand from a chair, sleep, work, exercise, care for family, use their hands, shop, drive, or leave the house. “Pain score 8/10” is important, but an FNP plan needs a meaningful functional target and a way to measure progress.

Part 2 — Do Not Miss the Mimics and Emergencies

Acute monoarthritis with warmth, swelling, marked pain, fever, or systemic illness requires consideration of septic arthritis and urgent evaluation. Crystal arthritis, inflammatory arthritis, fracture, hemarthrosis, tendon/ligament injury, avascular necrosis, referred pain from the spine/hip, and malignancy may also mimic or coexist with OA. A red, hot, rapidly swollen joint should not be treated as a routine “arthritis flare” with a refill alone.

Examine the joint and the person: gait, alignment, active/passive range of motion, effusion, tenderness, warmth/erythema, stability, strength, neurovascular status, adjacent joints, spine/hip when relevant, and fall risk. History of trauma, anticoagulation, immunosuppression, infection, inflammatory disease, and cancer changes urgency and differential diagnosis.

Part 3 — Core Nonoperative Management

Exercise is a central OA treatment, not an optional add-on. Strengthening, aerobic, aquatic, balance, range-of-motion, tai chi, and individualized physical-therapy programs can improve pain, confidence, and function when matched to ability and safety. Encourage activity within tolerance rather than prolonged avoidance. For patients with overweight or obesity, respectful weight-management support may reduce joint load and improve overall cardiometabolic health; it should never be used to withhold symptom care.

Self-management education, pacing, heat/cold strategies, joint protection, sleep support, walking aids, braces, footwear modification, occupational therapy for hand function, and home-safety changes may make the difference between a plan on paper and a safer life. Ask about transportation, insurance, language, stigma, caregiving, and ability to attend therapy or obtain a cane/bracing.

Part 4 — Medication and Procedure Safety

Medication selection is individualized by joint site, comorbidities, kidney/liver/GI/cardiovascular risk, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, falls, sedation, drug interactions, and patient preference. Topical and oral therapies have different risk-benefit profiles. Reconcile OTC NSAIDs, acetaminophen-containing products, supplements, alcohol exposure, and duplicate agents. Medication should support function and participation in active care, not become an indefinite substitute for reassessment.

Intra-articular corticosteroid injections may be considered for selected patients as part of a broader plan; procedural competence, diagnosis certainty, infection exclusion, glucose considerations, anticoagulation context, and surgical timing matter. Do not inject a joint when septic arthritis is possible. Avoid promising that any injection “rebuilds cartilage” or guarantees avoidance of surgery.

Part 5 — Imaging and Referral

Plain weight-bearing radiographs can be useful when the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms are substantial, trauma or another condition is suspected, or surgical planning is being considered. MRI is not a routine requirement for typical OA. Treat the patient, not an incidental imaging phrase: radiographic OA may be painless, and severe pain may have another source.

Consider orthopedic consultation when pain, stiffness, deformity, or functional limitation substantially affects quality of life despite appropriate core nonoperative care and the patient wishes to discuss surgery. Preoperative optimization may include tobacco treatment, diabetes and blood-pressure care, medication/anticoagulation planning, nutrition, dental/infection considerations according to local practice, falls prevention, caregiver/home planning, and realistic recovery goals. Referral is shared decision making, not a declaration of failure.

Clinical Case

A 72-year-old with knee OA has difficulty rising from a chair and has stopped walking because of pain. The patient has CKD, is taking an anticoagulant for AF, uses OTC ibuprofen daily, and cannot attend in-person PT because of transportation.

FNP reasoning: assess joint pattern and exclude acute red flags, then define function and fall risk. Daily ibuprofen plus CKD and anticoagulation raises medication-safety concerns. Build an accessible plan: review safer alternatives within the patient’s context, arrange telehealth/home/community rehabilitation options if available, address mobility aids and weight/sleep goals, and reassess whether symptoms remain quality-of-life limiting enough for orthopedic discussion.

FNP OA Framework

  1. Confirm the pattern: joint-specific symptoms, examination, function, and selective imaging.
  2. Exclude danger: hot swollen joint/systemic illness, trauma/fracture, neurovascular concern, inflammatory/crystal disease, or alternative diagnosis.
  3. Set functional goals: walking, stairs, chair transfer, work, sleep, hand use, independence, and fall prevention.
  4. Use core care: exercise/rehabilitation, self-management, weight support when relevant, devices/bracing, and accessible coaching.
  5. Escalate thoughtfully: medication/procedure safety, specialty input, and surgical consultation when quality of life remains substantially limited.

High-Yield Summary

OA: is a clinical and functional syndrome, not merely an x-ray diagnosis.
Urgent warning: acute hot swollen joint with systemic illness may be septic arthritis—not routine OA.
Core treatment: exercise, self-management, functional goal setting, weight support when relevant, and devices/rehabilitation.
Medication: needs kidney/GI/CV, anticoagulation, interaction, sedation, and functional-benefit review.
Referral: is reasonable when core care does not adequately control quality-of-life limiting pain/function and the patient wants to discuss options.
FNP standard: treat function, safety, and the whole person—not pain score or x-ray alone.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Joint examination, imaging, medication/injection decisions, infection evaluation, therapy, surgical referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, collaboration/scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
